title: The Teacher Finds Toil and Wisdom Frustrating
summary_text: The Teacher, David's son and king in Jerusalem, calls all things futile and asks what people gain from work. People come and go while the sun, wind, and rivers follow the same paths. Eyes and ears never have enough, and what seems new has happened before. Those who come later forget earlier lives. The Teacher uses his great wisdom to study life but finds it like chasing wind, with more knowledge bringing more grief.
key_points: The Teacher calls everything futile and questions what human labor gains.
Nature repeats its movements while generations pass, desires remain unsatisfied, and earlier lives are forgotten.
The Teacher's search through wisdom finds human activity frustrating and unable to straighten what is crooked.
Examining wisdom, madness, and folly leaves him with more sorrow as knowledge increases.

title: Pleasure and Achievement Cannot Escape Death
summary_text: The Teacher tests pleasure through wine, great building works, gardens, servants, riches, music, and many concubines. He enjoys his labor but finds no lasting gain when he looks back at all he has achieved. Wisdom is better than folly, yet wise and foolish people both die and are forgotten. He despairs because someone who did not work for his wealth will inherit it and may be foolish. He then describes enjoying food, drink, and work as God's gift, contrasting God's gifts to those who please Him with the sinner's task of gathering for others.
key_points: The Teacher gathers pleasures, possessions, servants, and great works, yet finds the results like chasing wind.
Wisdom exceeds folly, but death and forgetfulness come to both wise and foolish people.
Leaving hard-earned wealth to an unknown successor makes the Teacher despair over his labor.
Enjoyment comes from God, who gives wisdom and joy to those pleasing Him and gathering work to the sinner.

title: Human Times and God's Enduring Work
summary_text: A poem places birth and death, grief and joy, war and peace within their appointed times. The Teacher says God makes everything beautiful in its time and puts eternity in human hearts, yet people cannot grasp His whole work. Enjoying life and work is God's gift, and His lasting deeds call for fear of Him. Seeing wickedness where judgment belongs, the Teacher says God will judge righteous and wicked people. He then considers humans and animals sharing death and dust, questions where their spirits go, and returns to enjoying one's work.
key_points: Different human activities and experiences, from birth and death to war and peace, each have their time.
People cannot grasp God's whole work, but enjoyment is His gift and His enduring deeds call for reverence.
Despite wickedness in places of judgment, God will judge both the righteous and the wicked.
Humans and animals share death and dust, and the Teacher questions where their spirits go before commending enjoyment of work.

title: Oppression, Lonely Toil, and the Need for Companions
summary_text: The Teacher sees oppressed people weeping with no one to comfort them and calls the dead, and even the unborn, better off. He sees envy behind success but also warns that idle hands bring ruin. A lone worker keeps gaining wealth with no one to share it and no joy in it. Friends can lift, warm, and defend each other. A poor, wise youth can replace a foolish king, yet even this new king will lose the praise of those who come later.
key_points: The powerless have no comforter, leading the Teacher to call the dead and unborn better off than the living.
Envious labor, destructive idleness, and a solitary worker's endless wealth-gathering show the frustration of work without rest or enjoyment.
Companions help after a fall, provide warmth, and resist attack more effectively than someone alone.
A wise youth can rise from poverty and prison to replace a foolish king, but later people will not celebrate him.

title: Fear God and Receive Enjoyment as His Gift

Money cannot satisfy those who love it, can rob its owner of sleep, and may cause harm or be lost, while death leaves no wealth to carry away. He ends by calling the joy found in food, drink, wealth, and work a gift from God.

title: Wealth and Long Life Without Enjoyment
summary_text: The Teacher sees a man given wealth and honor by God who cannot enjoy them, while a stranger does. Many children and a long life do not help if the man finds no joy and is not properly buried. The Teacher calls a stillborn child better off, with more rest than that man. Work feeds the mouth but never fills desire, and what one has is better than wandering wishes. He ends by asking who knows what is good in a brief life or what will come after it.
key_points: A person may receive wealth from God but lack enjoyment while a stranger benefits from it.
The Teacher calls a stillborn child more at rest than a long-lived, prosperous person without satisfaction or burial.
Work does not end appetite, and visible possessions are better than wandering desire.
More words do not solve human limits, and no one can explain life's good or predict what follows it.

title: Wisdom Faces Sorrow and Its Own Limits
summary_text: The Teacher values mourning, wise rebuke, and patience above empty pleasure, pride, and anger. He sees the righteous die and the wicked live long, warns against being too righteous or wise and too wicked or foolish, and says those fearing God heed both warnings. No one is free from sin, and wisdom stays beyond his reach. He describes a woman who traps the sinner, while one pleasing God escapes. In his search he found one upright man among a thousand but no such woman, concluding that God made people upright but they chose schemes.
key_points: Mourning brings death to the living person's attention, and wise rebuke is better than foolish entertainment.
Patience is better than pride, wisdom shelters life, and God makes both prosperity and adversity.
The Teacher observes unexpected outcomes for righteous and wicked people and gives paired warnings to be held with fear of God.
Wisdom gives strength, but everyone sins and has reason to remember their own curses before reacting to others' words.
The Teacher's unfinished search describes a woman's trap and rare uprightness, ending with humanity's schemes despite God's upright creation.
